structured_output.summary: Reviewed the new cross-OS reset harness (tests/support/cross_os_reset.rs, src/runner/linux/journal/cross_os.rs, the journal unit-test module, and the native fixture slices) against the stated fault requirements. No product safety bug found: the journal/installation logic is sound as exercised, and the harness does test the real properties rather than mocks. Specifically, the guest-reset rejections are meaningful — with the SQLite renamed away and attachment/anchor.json removed, a regression that treated a missing anchor as standalone would make validate_store return the (None, None) => Ok(()) branch, so the assertion genuinely catches it; the corrupt-anchor case correctly re-applies 0o600 first so it exercises the JSON path and not owned()'s permission check. The retention property has real teeth: the empty ReconcileBegin/ReconcileCommit pair must be Rejected while the Linux boundary is still populated and unsealed, and the grant is only cleared after a cleanup derived from the actual Journal::cleanup seal, whose boundary_sha256 is checked against the coordinator-issued intent. Structural choices are correct: Subject is declared after temp/daemon so it drops first (mailbox and daemon still alive during unblock), and the bootstrap client connects to the installed system daemon rather than the isolated fixture daemon, so wiping the fixture SQLite cannot free the bootstrap hold. Hard-kill cleanup is covered by the supervisor's heartbeat/intermediary_lost path. The findings below are test-faithfulness, cleanup/hang, diagnosability, brittleness and hygiene issues in the new code, plus coverage limits — several of which are consistent with the explicitly declared scope (no production Driver transport, no full guest daemon) and are recorded rather than charged as defects.
findings: Test faithfulness (moderate): the cross-OS attestations are largely hardcoded constants, so the native-side assertions on them are tautological. cross_os.rs publishes guest-reset-rejected.json with "populated":true, "unsealed":true, "store_reset_rejected":true, "missing_anchor_rejected":true, "corrupt_anchor_rejected":true as literals; live.json hardcodes "user_started":true; live-after-coordinator-reset.json hardcodes "populated":true (only "unsealed" is computed). Enforcement is still real, because a failed subject assertion panics before the file is published and the native receive() then fails, so this is not a false pass. But assert_eq!(reset["store_reset_rejected"], true) adds no signal, and the exported evidence bundle asserts outcomes it never measured. Publish computed values (boundary.populated(), the is_err() results, marker.exists()) so the artifact and the coordinator-side checks mean what they claim.

Cleanup hazard (moderate): Subject::drop calls self.publish(...), which unwraps both std::fs::write and std::fs::rename. Drop runs almost exclusively while unwinding from a native assertion failure, so any mailbox write error becomes a panic-during-panic and aborts the process. An abort skips the remaining drop guards — the ChildGuard daemon kill and the TempDir removal that is the only thing deleting mailbox/configuration.json (which holds the fixture pairing secret). Make the three unblock writes best-effort (let _ = ...) inside Drop.

Hang hazard (moderate): Subject::drop unblocks then calls thread.join() with no timeout, and invoke_supervisor's frame loop has no overall deadline of its own — it reads until EOF and then child.wait(). A wedged or hung wsl.exe therefore turns a native assertion failure into an indefinite hang with no watchdog. Separately, Drop only unblocks reset-guest.json, coordinator-reset-observed.json and cleanup.json; a native panic before ticket.json (e.g. the "reset Invocation was not authorized" path) leaves the subject blocked for its full 120 s phase timeout before the join can return, so failures stall for minutes. Bounded, but worth a join deadline and unblocking the earlier phases too.

Diagnosability: receive() asserts !thread.is_finished() and panics with "Linux bootstrap ended before {name}", then Drop does `let _ = thread.join()` — so the actual stillyard::Error from run_wsl_bootstrap (Unavailable/Protocol/InvalidSpec, the only thing that explains why the bootstrap died) is discarded. On that assertion the harness should take and join the thread and report its Err. Related: once the 60 s (native) / 120 s (guest) budget expires, the guard `Instant::now() < until` stops matching and the arm falls through to panic!("Linux subject {name}: {error}") reporting a bare ENOENT rather than a timeout.

Environment brittleness (fails closed, but opaquely): the native registration hardcodes owner_uid: 1000 while Configuration::validate rejects any anchor whose owner_uid != geteuid(), so a WSL default user that is not uid 1000 fails inside install_attached_from_file and surfaces only as a mailbox timeout. The subject already publishes manager.json first and should publish its uid there for the fixture to use. Same class: linux_path hardcodes the /mnt/ automount prefix (configurable via /etc/wsl.conf); CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR must be on a durable local filesystem or Journal::open fails deep inside require_durable_local_filesystem with no harness-level precondition check; and the Python snippet embeds the marker path with {:?}, whose Rust Debug escaping (\u{...}) is not valid Python for non-ASCII paths.

Assertion precision: the three core reset rejections assert only Store::open(...).is_err(), with the security meaning carried entirely by the message string. A regression that converted the InvalidState fencing check into an unrelated I/O or schema error would still pass all three. Match on StoreError::InvalidState / the "admission remains fenced" text. The journal unit test linux_executor_journal_never_reinitializes_missing_or_corrupt_history has the same bare-is_err() pattern across six assertions, including the duplicate-writer and wrong-anchor cases.

Coverage limit with security relevance: the TicketCleanup is assembled on the Windows side with user_code_released: true hardcoded and boundary_sha256 copied from the intent, and the non-Linux path feeds the coordinator a fabricated proof(&reset_intent) that it accepts. So the coordinator does not verify the executor's seal cryptographically, and the test demonstrates the correct sequencing of release-after-seal rather than proving that an early or fabricated release is impossible. Also, the real seal's possibly_released (which the subject does assert is true) is never propagated into user_code_released, so the executor-seal-to-coordinator-cleanup mapping is not exercised faithfully.

Coverage limit (consistent with the declared scope, recorded not charged): no guest-side bridge or transport participates. The Windows `machine` CLI impersonates the executor using the pairing secret, so ticket transport, session/sequence handling and reconnect-after-coordinator-reset on the Linux side are unexercised, matching the stated exclusion of production Driver transport freshness and the full guest daemon. Additionally configuration.executor_cgroup (/sys/fs/cgroup/isolated-reset-profile) is validated but never used — the subject creates its boundary under STILLYARD_TEST_CGROUP_ROOT — so the production cgroup-path derivation is not covered by this harness.

Coverage gap (small): only the installation anchor (attachment/anchor.json) is removed and corrupted against a live boundary. The executor journal's own anchor (attachment/executor/anchor.json) is exercised only in the unit test with no live process, even though Journal::check() re-reads it on every records() call and the harness is already positioned to cover the live-writer case.

Privacy/hygiene (low): the fixture pairing secret transits mailbox/configuration.json, created with std::fs::create_dir/write defaults in the Windows temp dir and therefore visible to every WSL distribution through DrvFs; the harness never scrubs it and it survives the abort path in finding 2. The evidence allow-list in finish() correctly excludes configuration.json, but ticket.json and live.json (whose Record embeds the full InvocationTicket, including grant_id, offer_nonce and the session identity) are copied into an env-chosen MR_WSL_FAULT_EVIDENCE directory created with create_dir_all defaults. Separately, each run leaves ~/.local/state/stillyard/bootstrap/<operation-id>/ on the guest containing the full serialized request and the --nocapture stdout/stderr, with nothing collecting it.
